data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The night-time urban heat island is a feedback-driven thermal trap: high thermal mass stores daytime heat, low sky view factor traps nocturnal longwave radiation, and reduced evapotranspiration eliminates a key daytime cooling sink; the cross-city gap is best explained by the interaction of street canyon geometry (sky view) and impervious surface fraction, which together determine the nocturnal cooling rate.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If any one factor (e.g., anthropogenic heat, wind speed, or city size) dominates the others, the coupled feedback model is unnecessary.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the cross-city variation is better predicted by a single variable like sky view factor alone, the interaction model is overly complex.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the feedback loop is weak because emissivity is low or wind speeds are high, the coupled mechanism fails to explain the persistence of the UHI.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The UHI is not governed by a single isolated factor but by a coupled feedback system. Impervious surfaces with high thermal mass absorb and store daytime heat. After sunset, the street canyon's low sky view factor intercepts outgoing longwave radiation, re-emitting it downward and slowing the cooling rate. Simultaneously, the lack of vegetation suppresses latent heat flux, ensuring more daytime energy is stored as sensible heat. The cross-city variation is best explained by the product of impervious surface fraction (storage) and street canyon density (sky view): cities with both high impervious cover and tall, dense buildings exhibit the strongest nocturnal UHI because the radiative trap is most effective and the heat reservoir is largest.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
